entries.25c23a0376e57e7f610705e6e5a95e5db4a3a147: <div sID="gen11560" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="64" osisID="Ps.64" sID="Ps.64"/> <div eID="gen11560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11561" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11562" type="x-p"/> This whole psalm has reference to David's enemies, persecutors, and slanderers; many such there were, and a great deal of trouble they gave him, almost all his days, so that we need not guess at any particular occasion of penning this psalm. I. He prays to God to preserve him from their malicious designs against him, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.1-Ps.64.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He gives a very bad character of them, as men marked for ruin by their own wickedness, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.3-Ps.64.6">ver. 3-6</reference>. III. By the spirit of prophecy he foretels their destruction, which would redound to the glory of God and the encouragement of his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.7-Ps.64.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. In singing this psalm we must observe the effect of the old enmity that is in the seed of the woman against the seed of the serpent, and assure ourselves that the serpent's head will be broken, at last, to the honour and joy of the holy seed.
entries.882b02a397814f9c94775b9bb63dd9ecb1bbd64d: <div eID="gen11562" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11561" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Malice of David's Enemies.</title> <div sID="gen11563" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear my voice, O God, in my prayer: preserve my life from fear of the enemy. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hide me from the secret counsel of the wicked; from the insurrection of the workers of iniquity: <hi type="super">3</hi> Who whet their tongue like a sword, <hi type="italic">and</hi> bend <hi type="italic">their bows to shoot</hi> their arrows, <hi type="italic">even</hi> bitter words: <hi type="super">4</hi> That they may shoot in secret at the perfect: suddenly do they shoot at him, and fear not. <hi type="super">5</hi> They encourage themselves <hi type="italic">in</hi> an evil matter: they commune of laying snares privily; they say, Who shall see them? <hi type="super">6</hi> They search out iniquities; they accomplish a diligent search: both the inward <hi type="italic">thought</hi> of every one <hi type="italic">of them,</hi> and the heart, <hi type="italic">is</hi> deep. <div eID="gen11563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11564" type="x-p"/> David, in these verses, puts in before God a representation of his own danger and of his enemies' character, to enforce his petition that God would protect him and punish them. <div eID="gen11564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11565" type="x-p"/> I. He earnestly begs of God to preserve him (<reference osisRef="Ps.64.1-Ps.64.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hear my voice, O God! in my prayer;</hi> that is, grant me the thing I pray for, and this is it, <hi type="italic">Lord, preserve my life from fear of the enemy,</hi> from the enemy that I am in fear of. He makes request for his life, which is, in a particular manner, dear to him, because he knows it is designed to be very serviceable to God and his generation. When his life is struck at it cannot be thought he should altogether hold his peace, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.2">Esth. vii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.4">4</reference>. And, if he plead his fear of the enemy, it is no disparagement to his courage; his father Jacob, that prince with God, did so before him. <reference osisRef="Gen.32.11">Gen. xxii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Deliver me from the hand of Esau, for I fear him. Preserve my life from fear,</hi> not only from the thing itself which I fear, but from the disquieting fear of it; this is, in effect, the preservation of the life, for fear has torment, particularly the fear of death, by reason of which some are all their life-time subject to bondage. He prays, "<hi type="italic">Hide me from the secret counsel of the wicked,</hi> from the mischief which they secretly consult among themselves to do against me, and <hi type="italic">from the insurrection of the workers of iniquity,</hi> who join forces, as they join counsels, to do me a mischief." Observe, The secret counsel ends in an insurrection; treasonable practices begin in treasonable confederacies and conspiracies. "Hide me from them, that they may not find me, that they may not reach me. Let me be safe under thy protection." <div eID="gen11565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11566" type="x-p"/> II. He complains of the great malice and wickedness of his enemies: "Lord, hide me from them, for they are the worst of men, not fit to be connived at; they are dangerous men, that will stick at nothing; so that I am undone if thou do not take my part." <div eID="gen11566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11567" type="x-p"/> 1. They are very spiteful in their calumnies and reproaches, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.3-Ps.64.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. They are described as military men, with their sword and bow, archers that take aim exactly, secretly, and suddenly, and shoot at the harmless bird that apprehends not herself in any danger. But, (1.) Their tongues are their swords, flaming swords, two-edged swords, drawn swords, drawn in anger, with which they cut, and wound, and kill, the good name of their neighbours. The tongue is a little member, but, like the sword, it <hi type="italic">boasts great things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.5">Jam. iii. 5</reference>. It is a dangerous weapon. (2.) <hi type="italic">Bitter words</hi> are <hi type="italic">their arrows</hi>—scurrilous reflections, opprobrious nicknames, false representations, slanders, and calumnies, the fiery darts of the wicked one, set on fire to hell. For these their malice <hi type="italic">bends their bows,</hi> to send out these arrows with so much the more force. (3.) The upright man is their mark; against him their spleen is, and they cannot speak peaceably either of him or to him. The better any man is the more he is envied by those that are themselves bad, and the more ill is said of him. (4.) They manage it with a great deal of art and subtlety. They <hi type="italic">shoot in secret,</hi> that those they shoot at may not discover them and avoid the danger, for <hi type="italic">in vain is the net spread in the sight of any bird.</hi> And <hi type="italic">suddenly do they shoot,</hi> without giving a man lawful warning or any opportunity to defend himself. <hi type="italic">Cursed be he that thus smites his neighbour secretly</hi> in his reputation, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.24">Deut. xxvii. 24</reference>. There is no guard against a pass made by a false tongue. (5.) Herein <hi type="italic">they fear not,</hi> that is, they are confident of their success, and doubt not but by these methods they shall gain the point which their malice aims at. Or, rather, they fear not the wrath of God, which they will be the portion of a false tongue. They are impudent and daring in the mischief they do to good people, as if they must never be called to an account for it. <div eID="gen11567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11568" type="x-p"/> 2. They are very close and very resolute in their malicious projects, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.5">v. 5</reference>. (1.) They strengthen and corroborate themselves and one another in this evil matter, and by joining together in it they make one another the more bitter and the more bold. <hi type="italic">Fortiter calumniari, aliquid adhærebit—Lay on an abundance of reproach; part will be sure to stick.</hi> It is bad to do a wrong thing, but worse to encourage ourselves and one another in doing it; this is doing the devil's work for him. It is a sign that the heart is hardened to the highest degree when it is thus fully set to do evil and fears no colours. It is the office of conscience to discourage men in an evil matter, but, when that is baffled, the case is desperate. (2.) They consult with themselves and one another how to do the most mischief and most effectually: <hi type="italic">They commune of laying snares privily.</hi> All their communion is in sin and all their communication is how to sin securely. They hold councils of war for finding out the most effectual expedients to do mischief; every snare they lay was talked of before, and was laid with all the contrivance of their wicked wits combined. (3.) They please themselves with an atheistical conceit that God himself takes no notice of their wicked practices: <hi type="italic">They say, Who shall see them?</hi> A practical disbelief of God's omniscience is at the bottom of all the wickedness of the wicked. <div eID="gen11568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11569" type="x-p"/> 3. They are very industrious in putting their projects in execution (<reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">They search out iniquity;</hi> they take a great deal of pains to find out some iniquity or other to lay to my charge; they dig deep, and look far back, and put things to the utmost stretch, that they may have something to accuse me of;" or, "They are industrious to find out new arts of doing mischief to me; in this they accomplish a diligent search; they go through with it, and spare neither cost nor labour." <hi type="italic">Evil men dig up mischief.</hi> Half the pains that many take to damn their souls would serve to save them. They are masters of all the arts of mischief and destruction, for <hi type="italic">the inward thought of every one of them, and the heart, are deep</hi>; deep as hell, desperately wicked, who can know it? By the unaccountable wickedness of their wit and of their will, they show themselves to be, both in subtlety and malignity, the genuine offspring of the old serpent.
entries.591104e181b11342840052dd81153d993911dd5e: <div eID="gen11569" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Judgments on Persecutors.</title> <div sID="gen11570" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> But God shall shoot at them <hi type="italic">with</hi> an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded. <hi type="super">8</hi> So they shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves: all that see them shall flee away. <hi type="super">9</hi> And all men shall fear, and shall declare the work of God; for they shall wisely consider of his doing. <hi type="super">10</hi> The righteous shall be glad in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and shall trust in him; and all the upright in heart shall glory. <div eID="gen11570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11571" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, <div eID="gen11571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11572" type="x-p"/> I. The judgments of God which should certainly come upon these malicious persecutors of David. Though they encouraged themselves in their wickedness, here is that which, if they would believe and consider it, was enough to discourage them. And it is observable how the punishment answers the sin. 1. They shot at David secretly and suddenly, to wound him; but God shall shoot at them, for he <hi type="italic">ordains his arrows against the persecutors</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.13">Ps. vii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">against the face of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.21.12">Ps. xxi. 12</reference>. And God's arrows will hit surer, and fly swifter, and pierce deeper, than theirs do or can. They have many arrows, but they are only bitter words, and words are but wind: the curse causeless shall not come. But God has one arrow that will be their death, his curse which is never causeless, and therefore shall come; with it they shall be suddenly wounded, that is, their wound by it will be a surprise upon them, because they were secure and not apprehensive of any danger. 2. Their tongues fell upon him, but God shall <hi type="italic">make their tongues to fall upon themselves.</hi> They do it by the desert of their sin; God does it by the justice of his wrath, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">v. 8</reference>. When God deals with men according to the desert of their tongue-sins, and brings those mischiefs upon them which they have passionately and maliciously imprecated upon others, then he makes their own tongues to fall upon them; and it is weight enough to sink a man to the lowest hell, like a talent of lead. Many have cut their own throats, and many more have damned their own souls, with their tongues, and it will be an aggravation of their condemnation. <hi type="italic">O Israel! thou hast destroyed thyself,</hi> art <hi type="italic">snared in the words of thy mouth. If thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it.</hi> Those that love cursing, it shall come unto them. Sometimes men's secret wickedness is brought to light by their own confession, and then their own tongue falls upon them. <div eID="gen11572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11573" type="x-p"/> II. The influence which these judgments should have upon others; for it is done <hi type="italic">in the open sight of all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.26">Job xxxiv. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen11573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11574" type="x-p"/> 1. Their neighbours shall shun them and shift for their own safety. They <hi type="italic">shall flee away,</hi> as the men of Israel did from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, <reference osisRef="Num.16.27">Num. xvi. 27</reference>. Some think this was fulfilled in the death of Saul, when not only his army was dispersed, but the inhabitants of the neighbouring country were so terrified with the fall, not only of their king but of his three sons, that they quitted their cities and fled, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.7">1 Sam. xxxi. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen11574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11575" type="x-p"/> 2. Spectators shall reverence the providence of God therein, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.9">v. 9</reference>. (1.) They shall understand and observe God's hand in all (and, unless we do so, we are not likely to profit by the dispensations of Providence, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">Hos. xiv. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall wisely consider his doing.</hi> There is need of consideration and serious thought rightly to apprehend the matter of fact, and need of wisdom to put a true interpretation upon it. God's doing is well worth our considering (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.13">Eccl. vii. 13</reference>), but it must be considered wisely, that we put not a corrupt gloss upon a pure text. (2.) They shall be affected with a holy awe of God upon the consideration of it. All men (all that have any thing of the reason of a man in them) shall fear and tremble because of God's judgments, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.120">Ps. cxix. 120</reference>. They shall fear to do the like, fear being found persecutors of God's people. <hi type="italic">Smite the scorner and the simple shall beware.</hi> (3.) They shall declare the work of God. They shall speak to one another and to all about them of the justice of God in punishing persecutors. What we wisely consider ourselves we should wisely declare to others, for their edification and the glory of God. <hi type="italic">This is the finger of God.</hi> <div eID="gen11575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11576" type="x-p"/> 3. Good people shall in a special manner take notice of it, and it shall affect them with a holy pleasure, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.10">v. 10</reference>. (1.) It shall increase their joy: <hi type="italic">The righteous shall be glad in the Lord,</hi> not glad of the misery and ruin of their fellow-creatures, but glad that God is glorified, and his word fulfilled, and the cause of injured innocency pleaded effectually. (2.) It shall encourage their faith. They shall commit themselves to him in the way of duty and be willing to venture for him with an entire confidence in him. (3.) Their joy and faith shall both express themselves in a holy boasting: <hi type="italic">All the upright in heart,</hi> that keep a good conscience and approve themselves to God, <hi type="italic">shall glory,</hi> not in themselves, but in the favour of God, in his righteousness and goodness, their relation to him and interest in him. <hi type="italic">Let him that glories glory in the Lord.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.64"/> <div eID="gen11576" type="x-p"/>

entries.79d846ca25762006f0391905c42a0e733ae1e568: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6188"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 64</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.64.1-Ps.64.10">Psa 64:1-10</reference>. A prayer for deliverance from cunning and malicious enemies, with a confident view of their overthrow, which will honor God and give joy to the righteous.</title> <div sID="gen9465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6188"/><hi type="bold">1. preserve ... fear--</hi>as well as the danger producing it. <div eID="gen9465" type="x-p"/>
entries.491db251a1e52512c3f05d62c9672859742deb5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6189"/><div sID="gen9466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6189"/><hi type="bold">2. insurrection--</hi>literally, "uproar," noisy assaults, as well as their secret counsels. <div eID="gen9466" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c00d9bad373300e044584200dc177949ba7ac3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6190"/><div sID="gen9467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6190"/>3-4. Similar figures for slander (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">59:7</reference>).<div eID="gen9467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bend--</hi>literally, "tread," or, "prepared." The allusion is to the mode of bending a bow by treading on it; here, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.58.7">Psa 58:7</reference>, transferred to arrows. <div eID="gen9468" type="x-p"/>
entries.51a87701b7ac3870b6fb7dee0258c7995ad11d7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6192"/><div sID="gen9471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6192"/>5. A sentiment here more fully presented, by depicting their deliberate malice. <div eID="gen9471" type="x-p"/>
entries.893ec09a6295c698e4265f75a5531ef4710a4b70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6193"/><div sID="gen9472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6193"/>6. This is further evinced by their diligent efforts and deeply laid schemes. <div eID="gen9472" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7f0b1c0840b652f0642b9c986c688ed23a0be6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6194"/><div sID="gen9473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6194"/>7. The contrast is heightened by representing God as using weapons like theirs. <div eID="gen9473" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8dc0ff6a672ff451c8d68252216923e22ad9063: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6195"/><div sID="gen9474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6195"/><hi type="bold">8. their ... tongue to fall, &c.--</hi>that is, the consequences of their slanders, &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.10.2">Psa 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.16">31:16</reference>).<div eID="gen9474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9475" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all that see ... away--</hi>Their partners in evil shall be terrified. <div eID="gen9475" type="x-p"/>
entries.e02eb6261a826c28ba0610798171051cfa8f77e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6196"/><div sID="gen9476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6196"/>9-10. Men, generally, will acknowledge God's work, and the righteous, rejoicing in it, shall be encouraged to trust Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.10">Psa 58:10</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.64"/>

entries.546b637b9a0b2ceffdb4d3652747f0660106ba3f: <div eID="gen20653" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20654" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20655" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20655" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20654" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20656" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays for preservation from the wicked, <reference osisRef="Psa.64.1">Psa 64:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.64.2">Psa 64:2</reference>; whom he describes, <reference osisRef="Psa.64.3-Psa.64.6">Psa 64:3-6</reference>; shows their punishment, <reference osisRef="Psa.64.7">Psa 64:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.64.8">Psa 64:8</reference>; and the effect that this should have on the godly, <reference osisRef="Psa.64.9">Psa 64:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.64.10">Psa 64:10</reference>. <div eID="gen20656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20657" type="x-p"/> The title, To the chief Musician, or conqueror, A Psalm of David. The Syriac says, "composed by David when warned by Gad the prophet, who said, Stay not in Masrob, because Saul seeks thy life." Some think it was composed by David when he was persecuted by Saul; or during the rebellion of Absalom. But Calmet thinks it is a complaint of the captives in Babylon. <div eID="gen20657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20658" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20659" type="x-p"/> Hear my voice - The psalmist feared for his life, and the lives of his fellow-captives; and he sought help of God. He prayed, and he lifted up his voice; and thus showed his earnestness.
entries.4d73697bf37bd1df852203b172e1b7d0888d8591: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20660" type="x-p"/> Hide me from the secret counsel - They plotted his destruction, and then formed insurrections in order to accomplish it. <div eID="gen20660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20661" type="x-p"/> Workers of iniquity - Those who made sin their labor, their daily employment; it was their occupation and trade. It is supposed that by this title the Babylonians are intended. See <reference osisRef="Psa.6.3">Psa 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.14.4">Psa 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.36.12">Psa 36:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.53.4">Psa 53:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.59.2">Psa 59:2</reference>.
entries.dfa14a52d74231abe81a27274039d2ab4788ed83: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20662" type="x-p"/> Who whet their tongue like a sword - They devise the evil they shall speak, and meditate on the most provoking, injurious, and defamatory words; as the soldier whets his sword that he may thereby the better cut down his enemies. <div eID="gen20662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20663" type="x-p"/> Their arrows - bitter words - Their defamatory sayings are here represented as deadly as poisoned arrows; for to such is the allusion here made.
entries.ea6fb31aa06b4f38c62eedd1f31a8aef8e2f4438: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20664" type="x-p"/> That they may shoot in secret - They lurk, that they may take their aim the more surely, and not miss their mark. <div eID="gen20664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20665" type="x-p"/> Suddenly - When there is no fear apprehended, because none is seen.
entries.bad36a7c060eebe6d5c826e723c8cd9687929d2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20666" type="x-p"/> They commune of laying snares - They lay snares to entrap those whom they cannot slay by open attack or private ambush.
entries.e2615663d42098301eb2c50433d7dea9870bfea6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20667" type="x-p"/> They search out iniquities; they accomplish a diligent search - The word חפש chaphash, which is used three times, as a noun and a verb, in this sentence, signifies to strip off the clothes. "They investigate iniquities; they perfectly investigate an investigation." Most energetically translated by the old Psalter: Thai ransaked wickednesses: thai failled ransakand in ransaking. To ransack signifies to search every corner, to examine things part by part, to turn over every leaf, to leave no hole or cranny unexplored. But the word investigate fully expresses the meaning of the term, as it comes either from in, taken privately, and vestire, to clothe, stripping the man bare, that he may be exposed to all shame, and be the more easily wounded; or from the word investigo, which may be derived from in, intensive, and vestigium, the footstep or track of man or beast. A metaphor from hunting the stag; as the slot, or mark of his foot, is diligently sought out, in order to find whither he is gone, and whether he is old or young, for huntsmen can determine the age by the slot. Tuberville, in his Treatise on Hunting, gives rules to form this judgment, To this the next verse seems to refer.
entries.1824143a0af0be5c69bcd3f89b3554deb9df0747: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20668" type="x-p"/> But God shall shoot at them with an arrow - They endeavor to trace me out, that they may shoot me; but God will shoot at them. This, if the Psalm refer to the times of David, seems to be prophetic of Saul's death. The archers pressed upon him, and sorely wounded him with their arrows. <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">1Sam 31:3</reference>.
entries.193b4d6a6f36d2695c8d7404c5c4840cdecdb3d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20669" type="x-p"/> Their own tongue to fall upon them-selves - All the plottings, counsels, and curses, they have formed against me, shall come upon themselves.
entries.243ab2c3f74c9695e3c276988b0ddbf09387c6be: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20670" type="x-p"/> And all men shall fear - They endeavored to hide their mischief; but God shall so punish them that all shall see it, and shall acknowledge in their chastisement the just judgment of God. The wicked, in consequence, shall fear, and,
entries.08fb42399f68efeff2955500f99b6556522aca64: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20671" type="x-p"/> The righteous shall be glad - They shall see that God does not abandon his followers to the malice of bad men. The rod of the wicked may come into the herttage of the just; but there it shall not rest. Calmet thinks that this is a prediction of the destruction of the Chaldeans, in consequence of which the Jewish people became highly respected by all the surrounding nations. But it may be applied more generally to the enmity of the wicked against the righteous, and how God counterworks their devices, and vindicates and supports his own followers.  <chapter eID="Ps.64"/> <div eID="gen20671" type="x-p"/>

entries.5fd6190d84e9353c2c6c34b37684fe641f0d9ca8: <reference osisRef="Ps.64.1-Ps.64.4">Psa 64:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9634" type="x-p"/> The Psalm opens with an octostich, and closes in the same way. The infinitive noun שׂיח signifies a complaint, expressed not by the tones of pain, but in words. The rendering of the lxx (here and in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.3">Psa 55:3</reference>) is too general, ἐν τῷ θέεσθαί με. The “terror” of the enemy is that proceeding from him (<hi type="italic">gen. obj</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Deut.2.15">Deu 2:15</reference>, and frequently). The generic singular אויב is at once particularized in a more detailed description with the use of the plural. סוד is a club or clique; רגשׁה (Targumic = המון, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.10">Eze 30:10</reference>) a noisy crowd. The perfects after אשׁר affirm that which they now do as they have before done; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.140.4">Psa 140:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.58.8">Psa 58:8</reference>, where, as in this passage, the treading or bending of the bow is transferred to the arrow. דּבר מר is the interpretation added to the figure, as in Psa 144:7. That which is bitter is called מר, root מר, <hi type="italic">stringere</hi>, from the harsh astringent taste; here it is used tropically of speech that wounds and inflicts pain (after the manner of an arrow or a stiletto), πικροὶ λόγοι. With the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> לירות (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.2">Psa 11:2</reference>) alternates the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. ירהוּ. With פּתאם the description takes a new start. ולא ייראוּ, forming an assonance with the preceding word, means that they do it without any fear whatever, and therefore also without fear of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.20">Psa 55:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.18">Psa 25:18</reference>).
entries.063ff03133ab4ce912d425c6d95f3737cfc4e231: <reference osisRef="Ps.64.5-Ps.64.6">Psa 64:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen9634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9635" type="x-p"/> The evil speech is one with the bitter speech in <reference osisRef="Ps.64.4">Psa 64:4</reference>, the arrow which they are anxious to let fly. This evil speech, here agreement or convention, they make firm to themselves (<hi type="italic">sibi</hi>), by securing, in every possible way, its effective execution. ספּר (frequently used of the cutting language of the ungodly, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.13">Psa 59:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.27">Psa 69:27</reference>; cf. Talmudic ספּר לשׁון שׁלישׁי, to speak as with three tongues, i.e., slanderously) is here construed with ל of that at which their haughty and insolent utterances aim. In connection therewith they take no heed of God, the all-seeing One: they say (ask), <hi type="italic">quis conspiciat ipsis</hi>. There is no need to take למו as being for לו (Hitzig); nor is it the dative of the object instead of the accusative, but it is an ethical dative: who will see or look to them, i.e., exerting any sort of influence upon them? The form of the question is not the direct (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.8">Psa 59:8</reference>), but the indirect, in which מי, <hi type="italic">seq. fut</hi>., is used in a simply future (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.28">Jer 44:28</reference>) or potential sense (<reference osisRef="Job.22.17">Job 22:17</reference>; 1Ki 1:20). Concerning עולת, vid., Psa 58:3. It is doubtful whether תּמּנוּ<note placement="foot">תּמּנוּ in Baer’s <hi type="italic">Psalterium</hi> is an error that has been carried over from Heidenheim's.</note> is the first person (= תּמּונוּ) as in Num 17:13, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.18">Jer 44:18</reference>, or the third person as in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.22">Lam 3:22</reference> (= תּמּוּ, which first of all resolved is תּנמוּ, and then transposed תּמּנוּ, like מעזניה = מענזיה = מעזּיה, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.11">Isa 23:11</reference>). The reading טמנוּ, from which Rashi proceeds, and which Luther follows in his translation, is opposed by the lxx and Targum; it does not suit the governing subject, and is nothing but an involuntary lightening of the difficulty. If we take into consideration, that תּמם signifies not to make ready, but to be ready, and that consequently חפשׂ מחפּשׂ is to be taken by itself, then it must be rendered either: they excogitate knavish tricks or villainies, “we are ready, a clever stroke is concocted, and the inward part of man and the heart is deep!” or, which we prefer, since there is nothing to indicate the introduction of any soliloquy: they excogitate knavish tricks, they are ready - a delicately devised, clever stroke (nominative of the result), and (as the poet ironically adds) the inward part of man and the heart is (verily) deep. There is nothing very surprising in the form תּמּנוּ for תּמּוּ, since the Psalms, whenever they depict the sinful designs and doings of the ungodly, delight in singularities of language. On ולב (not ולב) = (אישׁ) ולב = ולבּו, cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.118.14">Psa 118:14</reference></hi>.
entries.9e24c9f105277827555e5a11aa2a2494ee21ca72: <reference osisRef="Ps.64.7-Ps.64.10">Psa 64:7-10</reference> <div eID="gen9635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9636" type="x-p"/> Deep is man’s heart and inward part, but not too deep for God, who knoweth the heart (Jer 17:9.). And He will just as suddenly surprise the enemies of His anointed with their death-blow, as they had plotted it for him. The <hi type="italic">futt. consec</hi>. that follow represent that which is future, with all the certainty of an historical fact as a retribution springing from the malicious craftiness of the enemies. According to the accentuation, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Psa 64:8</reference> is to be rendered: “then will Elohim shoot them, a sudden arrow become their wounds.” Thus at length Hupfeld renders it; but how extremely puzzling is the meaning hidden behind this sentence! The Targum and the Jewish expositors have construed it differently: “Then will Elohim shoot them with arrows suddenly;” in this case, however, because <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Psa 64:8</reference></hi> then becomes too blunt and bald, פּתאם has to be repeated in thought with this member of the verse, and this is in itself an objection to it. We interpunctuate with Ewald and Hitzig thus: then does Elohim shoot them with an arrow, suddenly arise (become a reality) their wounds (cf. Mic 7:4), namely, of those who had on their part aimed the murderous weapon against the upright for a sudden and sure shot. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.64.9">Psa 64:9</reference></hi> is still more difficult. Kimchi’s interpretation, which accords with the accents: <hi type="italic">et corruere facient eam super se, linguam suam</hi>, is intolerable; the proleptic suffix, having reference to לשׁונם (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.6">Exo 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.20">Job 33:20</reference>), ought to have been feminine (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>), and “to make their own tongue fall upon themselves” is an odd fancy. The objective suffix will therefore refer <hi type="italic">per enallagen</hi> to the enemy. But not thus (as Hitzig, who now seeks to get out of the difficulty by an alteration of the text, formerly rendered it): “and they cause those to fall whom they have slandered [<hi type="italic">lit.</hi> upon whom their tongue came].” This form of retribution does not accord with the context; and moreover the gravely earnest עלימו, like the הוּ-, refers more probably to the enemies than to the objects of their hostility. The interpretation of Ewald and Hengstenberg is better: “and one overthrows him, inasmuch as their tongue, i.e., the sin of their tongue with which they sought to destroy others, comes upon themselves.” The subject to ויּכשׁילהוּ, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.11">Psa 63:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.19">Job 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.7.3">Job 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luk 12:20</reference>, is the powers which are at the service of God, and which are not mentioned at all; and the thought עלימו לשׁונם (a circumstantial clause) is like <reference osisRef="Ps.140.10">Psa 140:10</reference>, where in a similar connection the very same singularly rugged lapidary, or terse, style is found. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.64.9">Psa 64:9</reference></hi> we must proceed on the assumption that ראה ב in such a connection signifies the gratification of looking upon those who are justly punished and rendered harmless. But he who tarries to look upon such a scene is certainly not the person to flee from it; התנודד does not here mean “to betake one’s self to flight” (Ewald, Hitzig), but to shake one’s self, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.27">Jer 48:27</reference>, viz., to shake the head (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.15">Psa 44:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">Jer 18:16</reference>) - the recognised (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.22.8">Psa 22:8</reference>) gesture of malignant, mocking astonishment. The approbation is awarded, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.64.10">Psa 64:10</reference>, to God, the just One. And with the joy at His righteous interposition, - viz. of Him who has been called upon to interpose, - is combined a fear of the like punishment. The divine act of judicial retribution now set forth becomes a blessing to mankind. From mouth to mouth it is passed on, and becomes an admonitory <hi type="italic">nota bene.</hi> To the righteous in particular it becomes a consolatory and joyous strengthening of his faith. The judgment of Jahve is the redemption of the righteous. Thus, then, does he rejoice in his God, who by thus judging and redeeming makes history into the history of redemption, and hide himself the more confidingly in Him; and all the upright boast themselves, viz., in God, who looks into the heart and practically acknowledges them whose heart is directed unswervingly towards Him, and conformed entirely to Him. In place of the <hi type="italic">futt. consec</hi>., which have a prophetic reference, simple <hi type="italic">futt</hi>. come in here, and between these a <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. as expressive of that which will then happen when that which is prophetically certain has taken place. Thanksgiving Song for Victory and Blessings Bestowed <div eID="gen9636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9637" type="x-p"/> In this Psalm, the placing of which immediatley after the preceding is at once explicable by reason of the ויּיראוּ so prominent in both (<reference osisRef="Ps.64.10">Psa 64:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.65.9">Psa 65:9</reference>), we come upon the same intermingling of the natural and the historical as in <reference osisRef="Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9">Psa 8:1-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Psa 19:1-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1">Psa 29:1</reference>-11. The congregation gathered around the sanctuary on Zion praises its God, by whose mercy its imperilled position in relation to other nations has been rescued, and by whose goodness it again finds itself at peace, surrounded by fields rich in promise. In addition to the blessing which it has received in the bounties of nature, it does not lose sight of the answer to prayer which it has experienced in its relation to the world of nations. His rule in human history and His rule in nature are, to the church, reflected the one in the other. In the latter, as in the former, it sees the almighty and bountiful hand of Him who answers prayer and expiates sins, and through judgment opens up a way for His love. The deliverance which it has experienced redounds to the acknowledgment of the God of its salvation among the most distant peoples; the beneficial results of Jahve’s interposition in the events transpiring in the world extend temporally as well as spiritually far beyond the bounds of Israel; it is therefore apparently the relief of Israel and of the peoples in general from the oppression of some worldly power that is referred to. The spring of the third year spoken of in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.30">Isa 37:30</reference>, when to Judah the overthrow of Assyria was a thing of the past, and they again had the fields ripening for the harvest before their eyes, offers the most appropriate historical basis for the twofold purport of the Psalm. The inscription, <hi type="italic">To the Precentor, a Psalm, by David, a song</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.75.1">Psa 75:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1">Psa 76:1</reference>), does not mislead us in this matter. For even we regard it as uncritical to assign to David all the Psalms bearing the inscription לדוד. The Psalm in many MSS (Complutensian, Vulgate), beside the words Εἰς τὸ τέλος ψαλμός τῷ Δαυίδ ᾠδὴ, has the addition ᾠδὴ Ἱιερεμίου καὶ Ἰεζεκιὴλ, (ἐκ) τοῦ λαοῦ τῆς παροικίας ὄτε ἔμελλον ἐκπορεύεσθαι. At the head of the following Psalm it might have some meaning - here, however, it has none.  <chapter eID="Ps.64"/> <div eID="gen9637" type="x-p"/>

entries.9a2f6b2924de81c71e2b6b763f61d9f8918c04b1:
PSALM 64
This psalm expresses the language of complaint and prayer. David, in order that he may incline God to compassionate his case, dwells upon the injustice and cruelty, the intrigues and deceitfulness of his enemies. At the close, his eyes are directed to God, in the anticipation of a joyful deliverance from their hands.
To the chief musician. A Psalm of David.
Psalm 64:1-6
1. Hear my voice, O God: in my prayer: preserve my life from fear of the enemy. 2. Hide me from the counsel of the wicked; from the assembly of the workers of iniquity. 3. For they have whetted their tongue like a sword; they have directed [or aimed
The original word דרך, darach, signifies to go, to send out, direct, and is used in different senses, according to the objects to which it is applied. “But most especially it is used of a bow or arrows. If of קשת, a bow, then it is to bend it; if of חצים, arrows, then it is not so properly to shoot as to prepare, or direct them. So Psalm 58:7, ‘He directeth or prepareth his arrows;’ so here, ‘they direct, or aim, or make ready their arrows.’ Parallel to which is that of Jeremiah 9:3, where being applied to the tongue, as to a bow that shoots out lying words, as arrows, it must be rendered bend; but here applied to words as arrows, direct, and not bend.” — Hammond
] for their arrow a bitter word, [or report.] 4. To shoot in secret at the perfect; suddenly will they shoot, and not fear. 5. They assure themselves in an evil work, they commune of laying snares privily; they say, Who shall see them? 6. They have searched out iniquities, they have accomplished a diligent search, [lit. a search searched out,] both the inward part of each of them, and the heart, is deep.
 
1. Hear my voice, O God! He begins by saying that he prayed earnestly, and with vehemence, stating, at the same time, what rendered this necessary. The voice is heard in prayer, proportionally to the earnestness and ardor which we feel. He condescends upon the circumstances of distress in which he was presently placed, and takes notice of the dangers to which his life was exposed from enemies, with other points fitted to excite the favorable consideration of God. His praying that God would protect his life, proves that it must have been in danger at this time. In the second verse, he intimates that his enemies were numerous; and that, without divine assistance, he would be unable to sustain their attacks. Some difficulty attaches to the words, from their being susceptible of two meanings. The Hebrew term סוד, sod, which signifies a secret, is understood by some to refer here to the secret plots of the wicked, and by others, to denote their meeting together for consultation. In translating it, I have employed a word which admits of either interpretation. The term רגשת, rigshath, used in the second part of the verse, may also be rendered in two ways, as meaning either an assembly of men, or noise and uproar. It comes from רגש, ragash, a root signifying to make a tumult. This would suggest that the word סוד, sod, in the former clause, might refer to the clandestine plots of the wicked, and רגשת, rigshath, in the latter, to their open violence; and that David prayed to be protected, on the one hand, from the malicious purposes of his enemies, and, on the other, from the forcible measures by which they proceeded to put them into execution. But the meaning first given, and which I have adopted, seems the most simple and natural, That he solicits the compassion of God, by complaining of the number that were banded against him. Still his language implies that he looked upon the protection of heaven as amply sufficient against the greatest combination of adversaries. I may add, that there is an implied plea for strengthening his cause in prayer, in what he says of the malice and wickedness of those who were opposed to him; for the more cruel and unjust the conduct of our enemies may be, we have proportionally the better ground to believe that God will interpose in our behalf.
